en: They will take you with your hands bound.
You have not accepted what I said.
You are determined to go, my sultan,
To the place where you will die in grief.
No good comes from the Kalmyks;
Their tidings are ill.
They should never settle beside us!
If they survive, you will see:
They will learn your secrets thoroughly.
If, grown strong, you will not heed me,
They will put an end to your quarrel.
They will watch your camp from afar.
If they survive, just wait—
They will make your fate known.
My sultan, do not keep calling him your true kin,
The man who merely winks his eye.
You keep calling him your true kin,
The man who merely winks his eye.
Can it be right to embrace
A kinsman whose belly holds deceit?
If those men keep you apart,
They will nail down your hands.
If they survive, they will show you
Sufferings no human head has seen.
We joined when I was small as a louse,
United when I was thumb-sized.
My king, my lord, heed my words.
I have said much: listen to reason.
My generous lord, listen to me.
Let us take the finest of the sixty,
The mightiest of the forty companions,
Our precious, trusted friends;
Let us send to the Kalmyks
Almambet and Syrgak,
Without letting a single person know,
Without showing a single person.
Let us send a force to intercept them;
Once we meet that accursed man,
Let us have him slain as a sacrifice
And secretly put him to death!
Those two will suffice if they go.
Let us reach him and sever his neck,
That enemy who has left his homeland.
My orphaned lord, heed my words;
Let us extinguish him like a fire!”
Then Manas bristled,
Bellowing in wrath.
His eyes blazed like a lion's.
That dear, guileless lion—
When did he ever heed Kanykei's words?!
His great teeth, broad as a door,
The leopard ground again and again.
The lord grew angry;
His bloodlust seized him.
“If I leave you to your will, my shrew,
You prance about,
Speaking of unimagined terrors,
Making my kinsmen enemies.
When my kin come, you call them Kalmyks;
You are openly stirring trouble for me!
Speaking in opposition,
You act as my enemy!
When has my sorrowful lot improved?
Driven far away,
My eight kinsmen
Vanished without a trace.
The four corners of the world
I searched four times without finding them;
My lordly person suffered disgrace.
I raised Akkula as my courser;
I endured torment for my kin.
At Zhelpinish, the end of the earth,
I searched for my seven elder brothers in vain.
On the road I suffered utter humiliation.
You would turn my hair white.
Always, my shrew,
You have left me alone.
If you keep on like this, you shrew,
You will dig my broad grave,
Set me against my kin,
And boil my bitter misery.
You begin slander and disorder.
You woman, you would show me
Strange troubles no one has seen.
You have worsened, you shrew,
An incurable sickness and calamity.
Upon my wandering, weary kin
You would inflict punishment.
You have spoken of a vile spectacle,
Making enemies before they come,
Reducing the households of my people.
Woman, you would make a spectacle for me.
You speak words of discord.
If you go on like this, you wretch,
You will make my kin my enemies.
My people who have come wandering—
You keep calling them Kalmyks.
If you do not stop this conduct,
You will leave this hapless head alone!
If I heed your words, woman,
The fostered bird will return to its land.
Will not my gathered people all flee
Back to the peoples they came from?
The harrier will return to its land.
Will not this wretched soul be left alone,
If my gathered people return to their own?
Speaking many stubborn words,
You have struck me with your speech.
Saying you will slaughter my kin when they come,
You have brought strange suffering on my head!”
Fuming and stamping in anger,
The lion khan thundered.
Generous Lord Manas's
Old warrior's whip—
Its broad leather fitting set with glass,
Its wrist-loop hung with ornaments.
Young cotoneaster from Opol Mountain
He had ordered cut in autumn
And turned into a whip-handle.
He had it soaked through with glue,
Covered in elephant hide.
The lame smith Bölökbay
Had fitted the handle with skill.
A whole gelded he-goat's hide
He had twisted for its core;
The hide of an unbred yearling
He had packed and braided tight.
Your khan father's warrior's whip—
Its stroke would deafen the ears;
When your mother spoke in protest,
That whip bent her backward.
Leopard Bakai Khan was there;
A broad council, a great assembly,
All forty companions were there,
Khan Koshoi of the Katagan,
Zhamgyrchy of the Eshtek,
And all their sons were there.
Your gray-maned khan father raged,
Paying no heed to the people.
The black-sided warrior's whip
He seized and swung about.
He plunged your mother into darkness,
Lashing out with a stroke.
My blackberry-patterned dress
Split along its pleats.
Your disgraced, shrewish mother's
Blood poured from her side.
My butterfly-patterned dress
Split along its side seam.
Your disgraced, shrewish mother's
Blood poured out dark.
For the time it takes to boil meat, this wretched soul
Lay senseless and weak.
A curse on being a woman!
Your unfortunate mother bled badly,
Sometimes able to come to herself,
Sometimes unable to regain her senses—
I, your ill-fated mother.
I had not suffered torment like this.
Like some worthless wife,
To your generous father Manas
I did not speak in protest.
I awoke from my swoon.
At your father, gone to the other world,
I did not so much as twitch a frown.
Without speaking, without a word,
I continued to serve him.
To your leopard father Manas
I made no objection.
Your father was not satisfied.
Of the six blades fallen from heaven,
Your father had taken Zulpukor.
He drew it from its sheath, looming over me,
To slaughter me as a sacrifice.
He was coming toward your mother
To cut off her head.
Hero Koshoi and the leader Bakai Khan
Stepped between us,
Preventing the sword-stroke,
Pleading for my life.
Almambet, son of Azyz Khan,
Seized that sword.
Even then your father would not relent.
“I will cut off the disgraced one's head!”
He roared, refusing to stop.
Your lion father, renowned among men,
Would torment this hapless head.
While your father behaved like this,
Your mother moved away in haste.
I, the shrew, beside myself,
Cowered against the yurt's lattice.
Unable to collect myself,
Distraught at what I had said,
Speechless with fear, my strength gone,
Chubak, son of Akbaltai,
Came to intervene.
Just as this was happening,
Leopard Bakai began to speak,
Speaking softly, laying down firm words:
“When you rage, leopard,
You are slaughtering your wife.
Is she your hostile enemy?
Generous one, what has come over you?
Your world was full and balanced;
You were a lion favored by the unseen patron.
You run with sword in hand,
Roaring as you charge.
Are the Russian people here?
Your prowess is beyond reproach.
To shout and take up a sword,
To split the rocks with your shouting,
To fly into a rage—
The Chinese people are not here!
White wheat submits to chewing, Manas;
A Muslim submits to restraint, Manas.
Be patient, Manas, be patient!
Do not play the wolf in your own camp, Manas.
Do not let your bloodlust seize you, Manas,
Against the wife who lies in your embrace, Manas!
If you truly are a khan, Manas,
Be patient, Manas, be patient!
Patience yields pure gold.
With patience you will excel;
Without patience you will fail.
If you keep feuding with your wife, Manas,
Should you live, you will come to ruin, Manas!”
At Bakai Khan's words your father calmed.
To that sword he had taken, alas,
Almambet and Chubak clung,
Intervening between us.
My generous lord spoke:
“For all manner of deeds I was driven out.
Wandering lost, this wretched soul
Went to Altai and was born.
Wandering, I found a land.
When I reached the age of twelve,
I found a land like broad Talas, Bakai;
I found a people like the great Kyrgyz, Bakai!
I took Talas and grew mighty, Bakai.
My father Karakan's eight sons, Bakai—
Not knowing their whereabouts, I suffered shame, Bakai!
A house built crosswise, Bakai—
When my kinsmen come to mind, Bakai,
This soul is crushed by grief, Bakai!
When I searched the face of the earth, Bakai,
When I sought my kin, Bakai,
From the desert of Mediyan, Bakai,
From a mysterious mountain ridge, Bakai,
It came to me in my wrath, Bakai,
This very Zulpukor, Bakai!
It was found by unseen providence, Bakai;
Through it my honor was protected, Bakai!
A companion until death, a keen blade, Bakai,
Zulpukor that enforced my rule, Bakai.
When drawn with a shout, Bakai,
It would not return to its sheath, Bakai.
